item.title: The Gift of Gratitude
item.description:
Gratitude

The Gift of Gratitude

Practicing an attitude of gratitude is powerful.

Posted November 22, 2026

Key points
  • Practicing positive noticing and thankfulness thinking is valuable anytime.
  • When we focus and savor, we strengthen and maximize the positivity.
  • Psychological science supports the value of gratitude practices.

Certain times of the year or milestone moments can increase the frequency with which we turn to appreciating the good, though this practice actually has value every single day of the year.

The positive psychology movement has helped individuals focus more on what is strong rather than only on what is wrong. As a therapist who works with individuals at various life stages and in situations of distress, I know and embrace the fact that we can’t ignore the overwhelming symptoms, heartache, trauma, and pain; however, I also believe that every individual has strengths and reserves of resilience that deserve to be incorporated and highlighted.

Source: Ralphs Fotos/Pixabay

Some people find this practice of being thankful and looking for gratitude moments to be relatively easy, but others find this much more difficult and unnatural.

Several tips are offered here for consideration to build the gratitude muscle.

Seeking Out the Good and the Good-Enough

Like the recent movement to incorporate more bloom-scrolling rather than just doom-scrolling on our phones, the notion of being on the lookout for more positivity can turn out to be a welcome shift for many. We know the gloom and doom exist, and we have plenty of opportunities to focus on it, but also actively seeking out more of the positive, the good, and the upbeat can be incredibly beneficial. Rather than dismissing the negative news or ignoring the overwhelming, we are making room for balance in our bodies and brains.

We can be in charge of our media meal plan and how we choose to budget our time and attention.

Source: Erik Karits/Pexels

The Big and the Bold—But Especially the Small

The idea of being on the lookout for gratitude moments is sometimes mistaken for waiting for those “big-ticket” items in life, like a windfall of money, a long-awaited vacation, or a promotion at work. While momentous moments are terrific, they tend to be rarer. However, the small moments of appreciating a delicious meal, a story about an everyday hero, a more scenic route home, the feel of a favorite blanket, or a beautiful bird on a branch are available to us on a much more regular basis.

There is a Japanese concept of Ma, which translates to the gap, interval, or space between things. This is often referenced in Japanese architecture, art, or conversation, but the notion of embracing space or pause can also be utilized in this pursuit of the positive. The gap or interval is not empty or useless; instead, it represents a meaningful void full of potential. So even in those moments between hearing difficult news, awaiting dreaded test results, or anticipating the next migraine headache, we can attempt to orient to something small, quiet, amusing, or pleasant for which we can feel grateful.

We can absolutely embrace the big, but we might as well also be on the lookout for the small because they are much more plentiful, readily available, and repeatable.

Source: Karina/Pexels

Go for the Glimmers

Being aware of possible triggers in our environment can have value and usefulness, but orienting toward noticing the glimmers internally and externally is often underutilized.

Glimmers are those small moments of calm or joy that can cue safety and relaxation for the nervous system. The notion of looking for glimmers was introduced by Deb Dana and based on work by Stephen Porges1, and this practice cues the body toward a state of safety and grounding rather than the fight-flight-freeze mode of response that is activated under threat.

Even on really bad days (or maybe even especially on really bad days), we can choose to notice some good or gratifying things.

Glimmers are the opposite of triggers; both exist in our world, and we deserve to be able to know how to be alert to both.

What We Focus on Flourishes

When we are actively looking for more positive, joyful, beautiful, interesting, or unique in our daily world, we begin to see more of it. Sometimes that elegant, sturdy tree, beautifully colored house, smell of our favorite beverage, or sparkling ray of sunlight coming through the window at a certain time of day has gone unnoticed until we take the time to notice. And once we notice, we tend to orient to seeing it again and again—along with that more satisfying sense of appreciation on repeat.

Focus helps with flourishing.

Source: johnhain/Pixabay

Savor the Moment

Orienting to some good news, a funny joke, the stuffy nose that finally cleared up, an enthusiastic pet greeting, or a beloved song on the playlist can all be wonderful in the moment, but what really allows the biggest benefit is to allow the positivity to fully soak in. Like attending to a spill on the counter, dipping a sponge into the corner of the spill for just a moment won’t be as effective as slowly, carefully moving the sponge around the spill to fully absorb the liquid.

When we pause to fully notice the benefits, orient the multi-sensorial delights, and stay with it for several moments, we are more wholeheartedly allowing the affirmative and encouraging to register in our systems. And if we choose to later repeat this positive moment in a journal or in a recounting to someone else, the benefits multiply and the positivity is reinforced.

Intentionally, mindfully staying aware of the positive is a happiness hack. And savoring the moment can be a superpower.

Psychological Science Support

Various research studies support the notion that optimistic, grateful people are happier, calmer, more empathetic, less stressed, have better physical health, and even live longer2. Neuroimaging results (MRI and fMRI) also show that practicing gratitude engages key brain regions involved in reward processing and emotional regulation3. These findings support the incredible connection between mind and body.

Source: Gabrielle Henderson/Unsplash

Studied gratitude interventions include gratitude journals, gratitude letters or texts, and other methods of counting more blessings than burdens. Although there are various self-administered psychological interventions that can improve overall well-being (such as spending time in nature, mindfulness, or acts of kindness), psychological science does consistently show that gratitude practices improve overall mental and physical health.

An Invitation

Even if this skill of looking for gratitude, positivity, and thankfulness doesn’t come easily or naturally to you, strive to refrain from self-blame about this. People have a wide variety of circumstances that can influence their ability to orient toward the good, and some of this is influenced by such things as external life circumstances and even genetics. The negativity bias in human brains is also well established and did have an evolutionary benefit4, but times are different now. A broader, more balanced perspective can help. And because brains are neuroplastic, practice in these skills makes for more permanence with these skills.

Be on the lookout for the lovely, and you, too, can optimize your inner optimist.

item.title: How 'Innocent Parties' Can Navigate Family Estrangement
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How 'Innocent Parties' Can Navigate Family Estrangement

These forgotten family members at the holidays need clear boundaries.

Posted November 22, 2026

Key points
  • Estrangement pulls uninvolved relatives into loyalty tests, message-carrying, and information-gathering.
  • Holiday expectations can turn separate, loving relationships into pressure to prove loyalty.
  • Refusing to discuss one relative with another protects trust without requiring one to take sides.
Source: Curated Lifestyle/Unsplash

The holidays are upon us, and with them comes the annual anxiety over family encounters. The messaging we receive is all about traditions, togetherness, and reunions, whereas many families experience grief, loneliness, and more due to estrangement within those families.

We go through it every year, and I can say candidly, as a therapist, it doesn’t get a lot easier. But whereas most of the articles and advice columns we read address the family members experiencing the friction—the son who won’t reconcile with his father, the sister who can’t forgive her brother—there are a lot of people gravely affected by the estrangement even though they do not actively take part in it.

These are estrangement’s forgotten people.

When two or more relatives cut off contact, the people caught in the middle often absorb the emotional fallout. They get pulled into triangulation in different ways, depending on the specifics of the family dynamics and situation.

Taking Sides

One of my clients, John, experiences this triangulation every year at the holidays. His mother and sister haven’t spoken to each other in years, having fallen out due to the sister’s choice of husband. John loves and is in close communication with both, and this works—more or less—during the year; but the holidays bring greater expectations of “togetherness,” and he feels forced to make decisions, none of which are satisfying to him. Does he choose one holiday party over the other? Manage somehow to rush from one to the other to make both parties happy? Eschew celebrations with both of them?

His mother and sister pull him into their dynamic by each pressuring John to prove his loyalty to each of them by attending their gathering. When he does, he feels forced to take sides, as each of them used the time to vent about the other. When he refuses to engage in this negative talk, there’s fallout from that, too.

Becoming the Messenger

Other families handle the triangulation differently. Rebecca’s large extended family has effectively shunned her cousin Peter after he came out as gay. But while they’ve cut off direct communication with him, they still expect Rebecca to act as the go-between, wanting to make sure Peter gets all their news and, again, passing on subtle negative messages to Peter through Rebecca.

Information-Gathering

Source: Kristina Flour/Unsplash

No one isn’t affected by estrangement, and families often seek to keep tabs on the “missing” relative or relatives. It can be as blatant as, “Where is Dad spending Thanksgiving?” or as subtle as, “Have you talked to your sister recently?” My client Ellen says this kind of questioning makes her feel like she has to edit everything she says, so that she doesn’t open doors to becoming the conduit, and so that she doesn’t accidentally betray any trust the missing family member has placed in her. Not exactly a jolly family gathering.

And the result is that the family member who is absent from the dinner table gets as much airtime as everybody else.

How to Avoid Escalation

It helps to remind yourself that you’re not the one who chose the estrangement, and you don’t have to be the stand-in family member. But as we all know, that knowledge isn’t going to make everything all right. Chances are, your people-pleasing tendencies get fired up now, and your choices need to be balanced with what you need and want, and how you want your own family to experience the holidays.

It may help to name the boundary you’re setting. “Remember, I spent last Thanksgiving with you, and I’m planning on going to Jason’s house this year. Maybe we can get together sometime next week to share leftovers.”

You Get to Decide

This may not have been the message your family of origin gave you, but it’s true for you now: You get to decide. You can set the boundaries you need, and you can reflect them calmly to family members who don’t want to honor them.

For example, you might say to the information-seeking family member, “You're both important to me, so I don't want to talk about either of you with the other. Now, tell me about what you did this week."

Pausing before answering can also be a great tool. When someone catches you off-guard with a comment or question about a missing family member, taking a breath may help you to not immediately try to smooth things over.

Things Can Change

Some mental-health practitioners encourage non-contact between family members who have fallen out over an event or a belief. That’s a topic for a different article, but I have to say that as a family therapist who works to improve communication, I’m optimistic that challenges within families are reparable to a point where agreeing to disagree and coming up with boundaries and limits can be incorporated into the family system and members can be in contact.

The invisible family members do not—and in fact should not—have to be the vehicles for reconciliation, but staying hopeful that it could happen will ease some of your feelings of frustration and resentment. Always staying open to that possibility can help you cope.

The Bottom Line

Source: Aron Thiwank/Unsplash

The best thing you can do for yourself in these situations is to get in the habit of establishing and maintaining the boundaries you choose and not succumbing to curiosity or hostility in the moment.

For those of us who want everybody to just get along—that’s good. Encourage your family members to meet with a mediator or therapist. It isn’t your job.

And always remember that it’s perfectly reasonable for you to have a close relationship on your own with each party and enjoy them for who they are.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
